title: Quantum and classical entropic complexity of the thermal state: coherence, decoherence, and the ergodic-to-localized crossover in random-matrix and many-body models
abstract: Does thermal averaging preserve signatures of eigenstate complexity? We study the entropic complexity C = S_1 - S_2 (Shannon minus second-order Renyi entropy) across the ergodic-to-localized crossover of three disordered models: the Rosenzweig-Porter (RP) ensemble, the power-law banded random matrix (PLBRM) ensemble, and the random-field Heisenberg chain. We compare a wavefunction-level quantity C_eig to the complexity of the thermal (Gibbs) state before and after pointer-basis dephasing, via the trace (C_tr) and diagonal (C_diag) complexities. The answer is mostly no: thermal averaging strongly suppresses, but does not eliminate, eigenstate-complexity signatures. C_eig develops a pronounced mid-phase maximum in RP and, at matching fractal dimension, in the structurally independent PLBRM model; a high-statistics scan resolves a weak (about 10%) but reproducible thermal shadow of this peak in the thermal diagonal complexity. This feature is confined to the two random-matrix models; in the Heisenberg chain the eigenstate complexity instead peaks at the many-body localization transition. A second, genuinely thermal feature, an edge just inside the ergodic phase, has no eigenstate counterpart and, in PLBRM, recedes with system size. Both features are tracked by scale-invariant crossover indicators: the log-ratio of the trace and diagonal crossover temperatures, which vanishes upon localization, and the relative entropy of coherence. Entropic complexity thus cleanly separates thermal-state and eigenstate physics: a sharp wavefunction-level feature, reproducible across unrelated random-matrix constructions, leaves only a faint, structurally distinct imprint on thermal observables.
summary: The paper uses entropic complexity to probe how quantum information encoded in individual energy eigenstates survives thermal averaging across disorder-induced phase transitions. It finds that while thermal mixing strongly suppresses eigenstate signatures, it also reveals a distinct 'edge' feature unique to the mixed Gibbs state, thereby cleanly separating eigenstate physics from thermal dynamics.
main_problem: The study investigates whether thermal averaging processes preserve intrinsic signatures of eigenstate complexity as a quantum system undergoes an ergodic-to-localized crossover.
main_result: Thermal averaging strongly suppresses the characteristic mid-phase peaks found in individual eigenstates, suggesting that the two types of complexity features (eigenstate vs. thermal) are governed by distinct physical mechanisms.
method: The authors employ entropic complexity measures ($C = S_1 - S_2$) applied to both pure energy eigenstates and the full thermal (Gibbs) state ($ho_T$).
model_or_system: Three disordered models are analyzed: the Rosenzweig–Porter (RP) ensemble, the Power-law banded random matrix (PLBRM), and the Random-field Heisenberg chain. These systems model transitions between ergodic and localized quantum regimes.
key_observables: Entropic complexity ($C$), Eigenstate Complexity ($	ext{Ceig}$), Trace complexity ($C_{	ext{tr}}$), Diagonal complexity ($C_{	ext{diag}}$), and the Coherence Gap ($C_{	ext{gap}}$).
important_parameters: Disorder strength ($\gamma$ in RP model), Temperature ($T$), and system size ($N$). The crossover is studied across ergodic, intermediate (multifractal), and localized regimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on comparing wavefunction-level quantities to thermal observables; specific approximations are used for calculating complexity in the microcanonical limit.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate temperature dependence of $C_{	ext{tr}}$ and $C_{	ext{diag}}$ (e.g., RP model), showing distinct features like a 'cold plateau' versus an interior peak, and show how PLBRM washout scales differently than predicted by independent assumptions.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares complexity measures across three models, identifying two key phenomena: a mid-phase eigenstate feature (seen in RP/PLBRM) and a distinct edge-of-ergodicity feature (visible only in thermal observables). It uses scaling indicators to separate these physical origins.
why_interesting: This work provides quantitative tools (entropic complexity) to distinguish between intrinsic quantum state properties (eigenstates) and the effects of thermalization/decoherence, which is crucial for understanding open quantum systems dynamics.

At γ = 3 (localized) both curves are single, coincident, broadened peaks. At γ = 1 (edge) Cdiag develops a peak above a residual low-T shoulder. At γ = 0.3 (ergodic) Cdiag has no interior maximum: it rises to a cold plateau as T →0 (the ground-state site complexity) while Ctr remains a clean interior peak. Temperature is in bandwidth units θW = T/Weff.
